questions.topic: Term Frequency Saturation: The Role of k1
questions.question: What shape does the BM25 term-frequency component tf/(k1+tf) have as tf grows, and why is that shape wanted?
options: Linear and unbounded, because every extra occurrence is equally strong evidence
Concave and bounded, because each extra occurrence adds less evidence of aboutness
Convex and accelerating, because repeated terms compound each other's evidence
Stepwise and flat, because only the very first occurrence carries any evidence at all

questions.topic: Term Frequency Saturation: The Role of k1
questions.question: Which two familiar scoring behaviors do the extreme settings k1 = 0 and k1 approaching infinity recover?
options: Pure idf weighting at zero, and pure length normalization at infinity
Cosine similarity at zero, and probabilistic ranking at infinity
Full length normalization at zero, and binary term presence at infinity
Binary term presence at zero, and nearly linear raw tf scoring at infinity

questions.topic: Term Frequency Saturation: The Role of k1
questions.question: With k1 = 1.2, a term's saturation value is about 0.45 at tf = 1 and about 0.63 at tf = 2. What does this pair of numbers illustrate?
options: Going from one occurrence to two adds less than the first occurrence did
Going from one occurrence to two roughly doubles the term's total contribution
Going from one occurrence to two is worth more than any later idf difference
Going from one occurrence to two crosses the saturation asymptote of the curve

questions.topic: Term Frequency Saturation: The Role of k1
questions.question: In the eliteness story behind BM25, what role does observed term frequency play?
options: It is the definition of eliteness, since elite documents are those with high counts
It is a nuisance variable that the 2-Poisson mixture integrates out completely
It is noisy evidence about a hidden binary property, eliteness for that concept
It is a direct measurement of relevance once divided by the document's length

questions.topic: Term Frequency Saturation: The Role of k1
questions.question: A spam page repeats a query term 100 times yet barely outscores an honest page with 10 occurrences, and loses to a page matching one extra distinct query term. Which structural property of BM25 explains this?
options: Common terms receive negative idf weights, which cancels out the extra repetitions
Length normalization divides the spam page's counts by its inflated total word count
Term frequency enters through a logarithm, so 100 occurrences count as about two
Each term's contribution is capped, while a new matched term adds a fresh idf weight

questions.topic: Term Frequency Saturation: The Role of k1
questions.question: You index short product titles where a term almost never appears more than once per title. How should this shape your choice of k1?
options: Raise k1 sharply, since the rare repetitions must be strongly rewarded when they occur
Leave k1 near its default, since with tf mostly equal to 1 the curve is barely used
Set k1 very high, since short titles need linear tf scoring to break their ties
Lower k1 to exactly zero, since idf must be suppressed for very short fields

questions.topic: Length Normalization: The Role of b
questions.question: In BM25, where does the length factor B = (1-b) + b×(doclen/avgdl) enter the score?
options: It multiplies the idf weight, shrinking rare-term evidence in long documents
It divides the final summed score once per document after all terms are added
It replaces the average document length whenever a document is unusually long
It scales k1 in the saturation denominator, effectively deflating tf for long documents

questions.topic: Length Normalization: The Role of b
questions.question: What do the settings b = 0 and b = 1 each mean for document length in BM25?
options: At 0 length is ignored; at 1 term counts are fully normalized by relative length
At 0 long documents are discarded; at 1 all documents are truncated to the average
At 0 term counts are divided by raw length; at 1 length only breaks scoring ties
At 0 the average length is recomputed per query; at 1 it is fixed at indexing time

questions.topic: Length Normalization: The Role of b
questions.question: The verbosity and scope hypotheses give opposite advice about long documents. Which pairing is correct?
options: Verbosity says long documents cover more material, so their counts need no discount
Verbosity says long documents repeat themselves, so their counts need discounting
Scope says long documents merely repeat themselves, so their counts need discounting
Scope says long documents are noisier, so their idf weights should be discounted

questions.topic: Length Normalization: The Role of b
questions.question: With b = 0.75 and an average document length of 500 words, what is the length factor B for a 300-word document, and what does it do?
options: B = 1.30, mildly deflating the document's term frequencies toward the collection mean
B = 0.60, deflating the term frequencies in proportion to the length ratio alone
B = 0.70, inflating the document's effective term frequencies as a concision reward
B = 0.45, roughly doubling the effective term frequencies of every matched term

questions.topic: Length Normalization: The Role of b
questions.question: In a search over API reference documentation, comprehensive pages that genuinely answer more queries keep losing to near-empty stub pages. Which parameter change addresses this?
options: Lower b, because length reflects scope here and is being over-penalized
Raise b, because the stub pages are exploiting weak length normalization
Raise k1, because the comprehensive pages need much stronger tf saturation
Lower k1, because the stub pages benefit from their repeated occurrences

questions.topic: Length Normalization: The Role of b
questions.question: A team re-chunks its RAG corpus from 1,000-token chunks to 200-token chunks without touching k1 or b, and BM25 rankings shift noticeably. Why?
options: Smaller chunks change tokenization, so the vocabulary of indexed terms differs
Smaller chunks make idf negative for most terms, flipping the ranking order
Chunk boundaries break phrase matching, which BM25 depends on for scoring
The collection's average length changed, so every document's length factor B moved

questions.topic: The Assembled BM25 Formula
questions.question: Which three components multiply and sum to form a document's BM25 score?
options: A term proximity weight, a query-length factor, and a document quality prior
A cosine similarity score, a length penalty, and a term co-occurrence bonus
An idf weight per matched term, a saturated tf factor, and length normalization
A collection frequency ratio, a linear tf factor, and a per-query smoothing constant

questions.topic: The Assembled BM25 Formula
questions.question: Why does the standard BM25 formula include the factor (k1+1) in the numerator of the tf component?
options: It rescales every term equally, so ranking holds and one occurrence yields full idf
It compensates for length normalization by adding back the score lost in long documents
It raises the saturation asymptote so that heavily repeated terms can dominate scoring
It corrects the idf estimate for terms that appear in more than half the collection

questions.topic: The Assembled BM25 Formula
questions.question: A short document with tf counts of 4 and 2 for two query terms outscores a document five times longer with counts of 10 and 6 for the same terms. Which explanation fits BM25's behavior?
options: The longer document's counts pushed its idf weights negative, reversing their sign
The shorter document matched its terms earlier in the text, earning a position bonus
The longer document was truncated to the average length before scoring began
Saturation flattened the extra occurrences and length normalization discounted the rest

questions.topic: The Assembled BM25 Formula
questions.question: A query term does not appear in a document at all. What does that term contribute to the document's BM25 score?
options: Exactly zero, since the sum runs only over the query terms present in the document
A negative penalty proportional to the term's idf weight in the collection
A small smoothed floor value derived from the term's collection frequency
The average contribution of the query's other terms, to keep scores comparable

questions.topic: The Assembled BM25 Formula
questions.question: What is the maximum possible contribution of a single query term to a document's BM25 score, no matter how often it repeats?
options: There is no maximum, since contributions grow with the log of term frequency
Its idf multiplied by (k1+1), the saturation asymptote times that term's weight
Its idf multiplied by the document length ratio at the time of indexing
Exactly 1.0, since the saturation function never exceeds one by construction

questions.topic: The Assembled BM25 Formula
questions.question: For the query `kubernetes autoscaling`, a document about `k8s` scaling scores zero in BM25 despite being highly relevant. Which inherent limitation of the assembled formula does this show?
options: Term proximity is missing, so adjacent matches cannot be rewarded properly
Query-side saturation is missing, so repeated query words are overcounted
Length normalization removed the document's only matching evidence
Scoring requires exact vocabulary overlap, so synonyms contribute nothing

questions.topic: Tuning k1 and b in Practice
questions.question: What are the widely used default values of k1 and b, as shipped by Lucene-based engines like Elasticsearch?
options: k1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75, a moderate saturation rate with strong length normalization
k1 = 0.5 and b = 0.25, a rapid saturation rate with slight length normalization
k1 = 2.0 and b = 1.00, a slower saturation rate with complete length normalization
k1 = 1.0 and b = 0.50, an evenly balanced setting used by most search engines

questions.topic: Tuning k1 and b in Practice
questions.question: What is the standard procedure for tuning k1 and b on a specific collection?
options: Fit them by gradient descent on click logs, updating the constants after each query
Derive them analytically from the collection's average document length and size
Increase both together until the average score of the top result stops rising
Grid-search both over judged queries, optimizing a ranking metric such as nDCG@10

questions.topic: Tuning k1 and b in Practice
questions.question: Search over meeting transcripts keeps surfacing the longest, most rambling documents at the top. Which single adjustment targets this symptom most directly?
options: Raise k1 so that repeated mentions in long transcripts saturate more slowly
Raise b so the verbosity of long transcripts is penalized more strongly
Lower b so that transcript length stops influencing any of the scores
Lower the idf floor so that common conversational words score higher

questions.topic: Tuning k1 and b in Practice
questions.question: Why does Lucene compute idf as log(1 + (N - n + 0.5)/(n + 0.5)) instead of the raw RSJ form?
options: The added 1 keeps weights positive, so a very common term can never reduce a score
The added 1 doubles the weight of rare terms, sharpening the ranking of long queries
The added 1 normalizes idf to the 0-to-1 range required by the saturation function
The added 1 corrects for documents added to the index after statistics were computed

questions.topic: Tuning k1 and b in Practice
questions.question: A team tunes k1 and b on a judgment pool built entirely from last quarter's most frequent queries, and metrics on rare queries quietly regress. What went wrong?
options: The grid step was too coarse to find the true optimum for the frequent queries
The metric should have been MRR, which is insensitive to the query frequency
The tuning set was unrepresentative, so the constants overfit the query head
The judgments expired, since the idf statistics change too quickly for reuse

questions.topic: Tuning k1 and b in Practice
questions.question: In a hybrid retriever, why is reciprocal rank fusion a more robust way to combine BM25 with embedding similarity than adding the two raw scores?
options: Rank fusion favors the BM25 list, which is more trustworthy than embeddings
Adding raw scores requires both retrievers to share one tokenizer and index
Rank fusion runs faster because the raw scores never need to be computed
BM25 scores and cosine similarities share no common scale, whereas ranks do
